issues.item: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these items are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. 'Story Feels Unreal' and especially 'Overwhelm on Recall' imply a disjointed, emotionally intense trauma memory, which fits the strong Memory↔Threat links. In contrast, 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests unusually easy narrative access to the trauma and directly pulls against the other memory items. For a severe PTSD profile centered on intrusive, overwhelming childhood domestic violence memories, this Memory combination is clinically inconsistent.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is incompatible with simultaneously being unable to put the event into words. This is a clear within-node inconsistency.

vignette: Amira's eyes would often glaze over as she polished glasses behind the bar, her mind drifting back to the memories of her childhood. She grew up witnessing her father's violent outbursts towards her mother, and those scenes still haunted her today. As a bartender, Amira had learned to be vigilant, always aware of her surroundings, but this hypervigilance came at a cost. She would mentally rehearse worst-case scenarios, imagining how she would protect herself if a similar situation were to arise (Worst Case Rehearsal). This coping mechanism made her feel prepared, but it also left her perpetually on edge. Amira's mistrust of others and herself was palpable. She couldn't shake the feeling that people were waiting for her to slip up so they could take advantage of her (Mistrust). This self-doubt seeped into every aspect of her life, making her question whether she was capable of doing the right thing (Self-Doubt). As a result, Amira became convinced that the world was a treacherous place, full of threats lurking around every corner. She began to notice potential dangers everywhere - sudden movements by others would put her immediately on guard, and she'd only feel safe in a very limited number of places (Threat in Movements, Safe Zone Only). When memories of the violent episodes surfaced, Amira felt overwhelmed by emotion, unable to process them without becoming frozen in fear (Overwhelm on Recall). She struggled to verbalize what had happened, as if the words were stuck in her throat (Nonverbal Memory, Cannot Find Words). These fragmented recollections only reinforced her negative self-appraisals, making her wonder how she could have let such things happen when she was a child. As the memories replayed in her mind, Amira's sense of threat escalated - every creaking floorboard or raised voice made her jump (Memory -> Threat). To cope with this perpetual sense of danger, Amira resorted to maladaptive strategies. She would repeatedly check that doors and windows were locked, trying to reassure herself that she was safe (Door and Lock Checking). However, these rituals only provided temporary relief, as the memories continued to intrude on her daily life. Amira tried hard to control her emotions, bottling up her feelings in an attempt to maintain a sense of normalcy (Emotion Control). As time went on, Amira's avoidance behaviors became more pronounced. She began to shun open or exposed spaces where she felt vulnerable, opting for the safety of enclosed areas instead (Avoid Open Spaces). Her hypervigilance made social interactions increasingly difficult, causing her to retreat from friends and family. Amira's divorce had also been a blow to her already fragile sense of self. She couldn't help but wonder if her ex-partner had left because she was somehow flawed or untrustworthy (Negative Appraisals). The memories of the violent episodes continued to haunt her, reinforcing this negative narrative about herself and her place in the world. In recent months, Amira's symptoms had intensified, making it difficult for her to maintain a regular routine. She found herself constantly on edge, mentally rehearsing worst-case scenarios and struggling to shake off the feeling that she was walking on thin ice (Maladaptive Strategies -> Threat). It was this suffocating sense of danger, coupled with her inability to silence the memories, that finally brought Amira to seek help - not just for herself, but for a chance to rebuild her shattered trust in others and in her own resilience.
